CT__Head / Brain:
The non-contrast CT head (NCCT) is the first-line imaging investigation in acute neurology and trauma — it is fast, widely available and exquisitely sensitive to acute haemorrhage and bone. In suspected stroke, its critical job is to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis. Interpretation rests on two rules: density (what is bright vs dark) and shape (the pattern of any bleed).
1WHEN TO REQUEST IT
NCCT is the go-to scan for the acutely unwell neuro patient. Core indications:
  • Suspected acute stroke — first to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis/thrombectomy.
  • Head injury per NICE rules — e.g. GCS <13 on arrival, focal neurological deficit, signs of basal skull fracture, >1 episode of vomiting, post-traumatic seizure, or suspected non-accidental injury.
  • Sudden severe thunderclap headache — ?subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  • Reduced GCS, and to detect raised ICP / hydrocephalus before a lumbar puncture.
Contrast is not needed for acute blood — it is already hyperdense.
2DENSITY: THE BRIGHT-VS-DARK RULE
Density is measured in Hounsfield units and read as brightness. Learn the two extremes:
Hyperdense (bright/white)Hypodense (dark)
Bone & acute blood→HYPERDENSE (bright)
CSF, air/fat, oedema, infarct, chronic collections→HYPODENSE (dark)
Crucially, blood ages on CT: acute haemorrhage is bright, becomes isodense (~1 week), then hypodense/dark when chronic. So a dark subdural in an elderly patient is an old bleed.

3SHAPE: HAEMORRHAGE PATTERNS
The shape of an extra-axial bleed tells you the source:
🧠Extradural
Biconvex / lentiform, does NOT cross sutures. Arterial (middle meningeal). Classic lucid interval.
🌙Subdural
Crescent-shaped, crosses sutures. Bridging veins. Acute = bright, chronic = dark. Elderly, alcohol, anticoagulants.
✴️Subarachnoid
Star-shaped blood in sulci, basal cisterns and fissures. Thunderclap headache.
💧Intracerebral / IVH
Bright blood within brain parenchyma or the ventricles. Look for surrounding effect.
Always then assess mass effect: midline shift, effaced sulci/cisterns, and hydrocephalus.

4EARLY ISCHAEMIC STROKE SIGNS
In the first hours an infarct may look almost normal — hunt the subtle signs:
  • Loss of grey–white differentiation.
  • Sulcal effacement (swelling).
  • Insular ribbon sign — loss of the insular cortex margin.
  • Hyperdense MCA sign — a bright thrombus in the vessel.
An established infarct becomes a wedge-shaped hypodensity conforming to a vascular territory. Remember: NCCT is used first mainly to exclude haemorrhage so thrombolysis can proceed — early ischaemia being invisible does not exclude stroke.
🚩
Call seniors/neurosurgery immediately for a large haemorrhage with midline shift, developing hydrocephalus, or signs of impending herniation (effaced basal cisterns, downward brain displacement) — these are neurosurgical emergencies. And remember: a normal CT does NOT exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage. If clinical suspicion persists, proceed to lumbar puncture at ~12 hours looking for xanthochromia.

🎓 Exam pearl. Two rules crack most CT head vivas: density — acute blood is bright (hyperdense), infarct/oedema/CSF are dark (hypodense); and shape — extradural = biconvex (doesn't cross sutures), subdural = crescent (crosses sutures), SAH = star-shaped in the cisterns. NCCT is done first in stroke to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis, and a normal scan never rules out SAH — always mention the delayed LP for xanthochromia.
A contrast-enhanced CT head uses IV iodinated contrast to highlight tissue where the blood-brain barrier (BBB) has broken down or vascularity is high — these areas enhance (become brighter). It is used mainly to characterise mass lesions, infection and some vascular lesions when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated. Remember: MRI with contrast is generally superior for brain tumours, the posterior fossa, demyelination and infection — contrast CT is a pragmatic first step, not the gold standard.
1WHY CONTRAST ENHANCES — THE BBB PRINCIPLE
IV iodinated contrast normally stays intravascular because an intact BBB excludes it from brain parenchyma. A lesion enhances when it either disrupts the BBB (tumour, abscess, active demyelination, infarct after ~5 days) or is intrinsically vascular / lacks a BBB (meningioma, vascular malformation). So enhancement is a marker of BBB breakdown or vascularity, not simply "badness".
EnhancesBBB breakdownHigh vascularity
2THE RING-ENHANCING LESION — THE KEY EXAM CALL
A ring of enhancement around a low-density centre is the classic finals scenario. The mnemonic is MAGIC DR: Metastasis, Abscess, Glioblastoma, Infarct (subacute), Contusion, Demyelination, Radiation necrosis / Resolving haematoma. The top three to distinguish are abscess, GBM and metastasis:
🦠Cerebral abscess
Thin, smooth, regular ring; central restricted diffusion (on MRI DWI); systemic sepsis features. Needs urgent antimicrobials + neurosurgery.
🦋Glioblastoma
Thick, irregular, nodular ring; crosses the midline via the corpus callosum ("butterfly" glioma); central necrosis, marked oedema.
🎯Metastases
Often multiple, at the grey-white junction, with disproportionate vasogenic oedema. Look for a known primary (lung, breast, melanoma).
In HIV, a solitary/few ring lesion raises toxoplasmosis vs CNS lymphoma (lymphoma tends to be periventricular, single, thallium-avid).
3OTHER ENHANCEMENT PATTERNS
Homogeneous, dural-based, extra-axial→Meningioma (dural tail)
Gyral / leptomeningeal enhancement→Meningitis, subacute infarct
Serpiginous vessels enhancing→AVM / vascular lesion
4CONTRAST SAFETY — CHECK BEFORE YOU INJECT
  • Renal function (eGFR/U&E) — risk of contrast-induced nephropathy; ensure hydration.
  • Previous contrast reaction / allergy and asthma/atopy — anaphylactoid risk.
  • Metformin — consider withholding around contrast if renal impairment (lactic acidosis risk).
  • Consider whether MRI with gadolinium would answer the question better.
🚩
A mass with significant vasogenic oedema and mass effect (effaced sulci, midline shift, herniation) or clinical raised ICP needs urgent senior + neurosurgical and oncology referral. Suspected abscess needs urgent antimicrobials + neurosurgery. Never give IV contrast without checking renal function and allergy history first.

The acute CT stroke protocol is a rapid, staged imaging workflow in a patient with sudden focal neurology. Its whole purpose is to answer three questions fast: Is there blood? (non-contrast CT), Is there a large vessel occlusion? (CT angiogram), and How much brain is still salvageable? (CT perfusion). Time is brain — roughly 1.9 million neurons are lost per minute of an untreated large-vessel stroke, so imaging must be immediate and must never delay a treatment decision.
1Non-contrast CT (NCCT) — exclude haemorrhage
The first and most important scan. Its job is to exclude intracranial haemorrhage, because management of ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke diverges completely. NCCT is also inspected for early ischaemic change:
  • Loss of grey-white differentiation
  • Loss of the insular ribbon (insular ribbon sign)
  • Sulcal effacement from cytotoxic oedema
  • Hyperdense MCA / vessel sign — visible intraluminal thrombus
ASPECTS 10 = normalLower ASPECTS = more established infarct
ASPECTS quantifies early MCA-territory ischaemia and helps guide whether reperfusion is worthwhile.
2CT angiogram (CTA) — find the large vessel occlusion
Contrast is given to map the intracranial and neck vessels and identify a large vessel occlusion (LVO) — proximal MCA (M1), internal carotid, or basilar artery — that is amenable to mechanical thrombectomy. An LVO is the group who benefit most from clot retrieval.
LVO on CTA→refer to thrombectomy centre
3CT perfusion (CTP) — core vs penumbra mismatch
Used selectively to estimate the ischaemic core (irreversibly infarcted) versus the salvageable penumbra. A large mismatch (small core, big penumbra) identifies patients who may benefit from reperfusion in the extended window — thrombectomy up to ~24h when perfusion imaging is favourable.
🔴Core
Dead tissue — will not recover regardless of treatment.
🟠Penumbra
At-risk but salvageable — the target of reperfusion.
4The treatment fork
Imaging drives a decisive split:
Ischaemic, in window, no contraindication→Thrombolysis (IV alteplase/tenecteplase, generally ≤4.5h) ± thrombectomy (LVO, up to ~6h, or ~24h if favourable mismatch)
Haemorrhagic on NCCT→NO thrombolysis — reverse anticoagulation, control BP, urgent neurosurgical review
🚩
Haemorrhage on NCCT means thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated. Never thrombolyse without first excluding blood and checking contraindications. Beware the posterior circulation (basilar) occlusion — it can look subtle on early imaging yet be rapidly devastating, presenting with reduced consciousness, cranial nerve signs or a locked-in state rather than a classic hemiparesis.

Learn the staged logic: NCCT (exclude bleed) → CTA (find LVO for thrombectomy) → CTP (core/penumbra mismatch for the extended window). Recognise the hyperdense MCA sign, loss of grey-white differentiation and a falling ASPECTS as early ischaemic markers, and remember time is brain (~1.9 million neurons/minute) — imaging exists to speed treatment, never to delay it.
A CT angiogram (CTA) of the Circle of Willis uses timed intravenous contrast to opacify the intracranial arteries, then reconstructs them (MIP / 3D) to map the anterior circulation (ICA → ACA/MCA) and posterior circulation (vertebral → basilar → PCA) and the communicating vessels. Its two headline jobs at finals level are hunting the ruptured aneurysm behind a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) and finding a large-vessel occlusion in acute ischaemic stroke.
1WHAT IT SHOWS & WHY WE ASK FOR IT
CTA is fast, non-invasive and widely available, making it the usual first vascular study after non-contrast CT. It resolves the Circle of Willis well enough to localise most aneurysms and occlusions, though digital subtraction angiography (DSA) remains the gold standard for small aneurysms and for planning endovascular treatment.
🩸Aneurysm in SAH
Localise a berry aneurysm to plan coiling / clipping
🧠Stroke LVO
Find large-vessel occlusion for thrombectomy
🔀Other vascular
AVM, stenosis, dissection, vasospasm
2WHERE ANEURYSMS SIT
Most saccular (berry) aneurysms arise at branch points on the Circle of Willis. Learn the classic three sites in order of frequency:
Anterior communicating (ACom)Posterior communicating (PCom)MCA bifurcation
  • ACom is the single commonest site of a ruptured aneurysm.
  • PCom aneurysms characteristically compress cranial nerve III.
  • MCA bifurcation aneurysms often present with haemorrhage into the sylvian fissure.
Multiple aneurysms occur in ~20%, so the whole circle must be scrutinised, not just the obvious lesion.
3THE SAH PATHWAY
A sudden thunderclap / "worst-ever" headache demands a structured work-up in which CTA has a defined place:
Thunderclap headache→Non-contrast CT (NCCT) first — blood in the basal cisterns
NCCT negative, still suspicious→LP at ≥12 h looking for xanthochromia
SAH confirmed→CTA (or DSA) to find and characterise the aneurysm
Key complications to know: re-bleeding (highest risk early — secure the aneurysm promptly), vasospasm / delayed cerebral ischaemia (give nimodipine), and hydrocephalus.
🚩
A painful third nerve (CN III) palsy with a fixed dilated pupil — or a thunderclap headache — is a ruptured or expanding PCom aneurysm until proven otherwise. Arrange urgent imaging and immediate neurosurgical referral; a confirmed aneurysmal SAH needs the aneurysm secured urgently to prevent re-bleeding.

Commonest aneurysm sites are ACom > PCom > MCA bifurcation. A painful CN III palsy with a fixed dilated pupil points to a PCom aneurysm, and giving nimodipine after aneurysmal SAH reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm.
CT venography (CTV) times an IV contrast bolus to opacify the intracranial venous system — the dural venous sinuses and cerebral veins — rather than the arteries. Its headline job is to confirm or exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), a young-person stroke mimic that is missed if you only think in arterial territories.
1What CTV shows & why you order it
CTV is the go-to when you suspect CVST. On a plain NCCT the clue is a hyperdense sinus (dense acute clot) or the cord sign (a thrombosed cortical vein). With contrast, the diagnostic finding is a filling defect within an otherwise opacified sinus — classically the empty delta sign in the superior sagittal sinus: enhancing contrast wraps around a central non-enhancing clot to give a triangular "empty" centre. The superior sagittal sinus is the commonest site, followed by the transverse/sigmoid and cavernous sinuses. MR venography (MRV) is the radiation-free alternative (favoured in pregnancy); a D-dimer may support the diagnosis but a normal value does not exclude it.
2How CVST presents
The picture is protean, which is why it is missed. Headache is commonest — it may be thunderclap or subacute and progressive. Other patterns:
  • Features of raised intracranial pressure — papilloedema, visual disturbance, an IIH-like picture.
  • Seizures (more common than in arterial stroke).
  • Focal deficits or encephalopathy from venous infarction.
Haemorrhagic infarct NOT respecting an arterial territory→think venous — get a CTV/MRV
Bilateral parasagittal / thalamic changes→SSS / deep venous system thrombosis
3Prothrombotic risk factors
CVST is a disease of hypercoagulability. Actively hunt these:
🤰Pregnancy / puerperium
Peripartum period is a classic high-risk window.
💊Combined oral contraceptive
The COCP is the exam-favourite trigger in a young woman.
🧬Thrombophilia
Factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid, protein C/S deficiency.
💧Dehydration
Especially in unwell or post-op patients.
🦠Local sepsis
Mastoiditis / sinusitis → cavernous or transverse sinus.
🎗️Malignancy / trauma
Paraneoplastic hypercoagulability; head injury.
4Management
The counter-intuitive core: anticoagulate.
LMWH acutely, then oral anticoagulationAnticoagulate even with venous haemorrhageTreat seizures & raised ICPFind & treat the cause (stop COCP, treat sepsis, rehydrate)
Yes — you heparinise even when there is an associated haemorrhagic venous infarct, because untreated the thrombus propagates and worsens venous congestion. Endovascular thrombectomy is reserved for deteriorating patients refractory to anticoagulation.
Duration of oral anticoagulation depends on whether a provoking factor is found vs an underlying thrombophilia.
🚩
Consider CVST in a young woman on the COCP or peripartum with a new persistent or thunderclap headache, seizures, or a haemorrhagic infarct that does not conform to an arterial territory. This needs urgent CTV/MRV and anticoagulation — watch for deteriorating consciousness and rising ICP, which signal a swelling venous infarct.

Two flags that scream "venous": a haemorrhagic infarct crossing arterial territories, and the classic young woman on the COCP / peripartum. CT Perfusion (CTP) tracks a bolus of IV contrast through the brain to build maps of tissue blood supply. In acute ischaemic stroke it separates the irreversibly infarcted core from the salvageable penumbra (tissue at risk but still viable) — the mismatch that decides who benefits from reperfusion. CTP does not replace the plain scan or angiogram; it sits within the stroke protocol as NCCT → CTA → CTP.
1The four parameter maps
CTP software models contrast passage to generate four maps. Learn what each represents:
CBF — cerebral blood flowCBV — cerebral blood volumeMTT — mean transit timeTmax — time-to-maximum
  • CBF and CBV fall in ischaemia; MTT and Tmax rise because blood arrives late and lingers.
  • Tmax > 6s is the usual threshold defining the hypoperfused (at-risk) territory; a relative CBF < 30% of normal defines the core on many automated platforms.
2Core vs penumbra — the mismatch
This is the whole point of CTP. The distinction is defined by whether autoregulation can still hold blood volume up:
💀CORE (dead)
Markedly ↓CBF AND ↓CBV — a matched defect. Volume has collapsed, autoregulation exhausted. Irreversibly infarcted.
🧠PENUMBRA (savable)
↑MTT/Tmax with relatively preserved CBV — autoregulation still maintaining volume. A perfusion–core mismatch = salvageable tissue.
Large mismatch (big penumbra, small core)→much to save → reperfuse
Matched defect (large core, little penumbra)→little to save → poor benefit, higher bleed risk
3Selecting patients for late-window reperfusion
A favourable mismatch lets you offer thrombectomy ± thrombolysis beyond the standard window, or when onset time is unknown (e.g. wake-up stroke). Two landmark trials:
DAWN — up to ~24h, clinical–core mismatchDEFUSE-3 — 6–16h, perfusion mismatch
  • Both selected patients with a small core and a large volume of salvageable tissue, extending thrombectomy to ~24 hours.
  • Without such imaging selection, benefit in the late window is unproven and risk rises.
CTP complements — does not replace — NCCT (exclude bleed) and CTA (locate the occlusion).
🚩
A large established core means little salvageable tissue: reperfusion offers poor benefit and carries a higher risk of haemorrhagic transformation. Always exclude haemorrhage first on NCCT, and never let perfusion imaging delay treatment in a clear early-window candidate — time is brain.

A large mismatch selects patients for late-window thrombectomy up to ~24h (DAWN, DEFUSE-3); a large core warns against reperfusion. Remember the order: NCCT → CTA → CTP, and CTP must never delay treatment of an early-window candidate.
CT__Neck & Facial:
A CT of the paranasal sinuses is usually a non-contrast, thin-slice study reformatted in the coronal plane, which best displays the ostiomeatal complex (OMC) — the common drainage pathway of the maxillary, frontal and anterior ethmoid sinuses. Its four core roles are chronic/complicated rhinosinusitis and pre-FESS planning, complications of acute sinusitis, sinonasal masses and trauma. Read every scan through four lenses: the appearances, the surgical danger anatomy, the hunt for orbital/intracranial spread, and the possibility of invasive fungal disease.
1Systematic review — sinuses & the OMC
Check each sinus group (maxillary, ethmoid, frontal, sphenoid) for aeration, then trace the ostiomeatal complex. Look for mucosal thickening, complete sinus opacification and bony sclerosis of the walls (a marker of long-standing chronic inflammation). Obstruction at the OMC explains recurrent maxillary/frontal disease and is the key target of surgery.
MaxillaryEthmoidFrontalSphenoidOMC
2Acute vs chronic — read the appearances
An air-fluid level within a sinus is the classic sign of acute infection (or recent lavage/trauma), whereas bony sclerosis and thickening point to chronic rhinosinusitis. Match the CT to the clinical timeline before calling anything infective.
Air-fluid level→Acute sinusitis
Sclerotic thickened walls→Chronic disease
Note: a small amount of dependent maxillary fluid can be incidental/post-lavage — correlate clinically.
3Pre-FESS danger anatomy
Before functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS), the CT is a surgical roadmap. Actively look for variants that put the orbit, optic nerve and anterior cranial fossa at risk of iatrogenic injury.
👁️Dehiscent lamina papyracea
Thin/absent medial orbital wall — orbital breach risk.
🔦Onodi cell
Posterior ethmoid cell abutting the optic nerve.
🧱Haller cell
Infraorbital ethmoid cell narrowing the OMC.
🧠Ethmoid roof / cribriform
Asymmetric or low roof — CSF leak / intracranial risk.
4Unilateral disease — think tumour or fungus
Unilateral opacification, especially with bony destruction or a soft-tissue mass, should raise suspicion of malignancy or invasive fungal sinusitis. In the diabetic or immunocompromised patient, aggressive unilateral disease is mucormycosis until proven otherwise. Add contrast CT and/or MRI to characterise soft tissue and assess orbital/intracranial extension.
  • Bilateral inflammatory change — usually benign rhinosinusitis.
  • Unilateral + bone erosion — malignancy / invasive fungal until excluded.
🚩
Features of orbital or intracranial spread of sinusitis — proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), reduced visual acuity, severe headache, focal neurology or signs of sepsis — are an EMERGENCY. Ethmoid sinusitis eroding the lamina papyracea causes orbital cellulitis / subperiosteal abscess; frontal spread gives Pott's puffy tumour; intracranial spread causes meningitis, subdural empyema, cavernous sinus thrombosis or brain abscess. Arrange urgent contrast CT/MRI, start IV antibiotics and involve ENT, ophthalmology and neurosurgery. Always consider invasive fungal sinusitis (mucormycosis) in the diabetic/immunocompromised.

A CT orbits is the first-line cross-sectional study for the eye and its socket, assessing the globe, extraocular muscles, orbital fat, optic nerve and the bony walls. In finals it appears for orbital trauma, orbital cellulitis, a suspected radio-opaque foreign body, and proptosis (thyroid eye disease or tumour). The single most exam-critical skill is separating the preseptal from the sight-threatening post-septal (orbital) pattern.
1Orbital cellulitis: preseptal vs post-septal
The orbital septum is the anatomical firewall. Preseptal cellulitis sits anterior to it — eyelid swelling only, with NO proptosis, no painful eye movements and no visual loss. Post-septal (orbital) cellulitis is a sight- and life-threatening emergency, usually spreading from ethmoid sinusitis across the lamina papyracea.
👁️Preseptal
Lid swelling only. White eye, full painless movements, normal acuity. Oral antibiotics.
🚨Post-septal
Proptosis, painful/restricted movements, reduced acuity & colour vision, chemosis. Emergency.
Proptosis + painful ophthalmoplegia + reduced colour vision→orbital cellulitis until proven otherwise
CT hallmarks of the post-septal form: orbital fat stranding, a subperiosteal abscess hugging the lamina papyracea, and possible intracranial extension (cavernous sinus thrombosis).
2Blowout fracture
Blunt trauma raises intra-orbital pressure and blows out the weak orbital floor (or medial wall). Look for:
  • The teardrop sign — herniated fat/inferior rectus hanging into the maxillary sinus.
  • Orbital emphysema (air tracking into the orbit).
  • Inferior rectus entrapment → restricted upgaze and vertical diplopia.
  • Test infraorbital nerve sensation — cheek numbness is a classic sign.
Child, minimal bruising, can't look up, bradycardia/vomiting→"white-eyed" trapdoor + oculocardiac reflex — urgent repair
3Foreign body & the MRI caution
CT is excellent for radio-opaque foreign bodies (metal, glass, stone). If there is any possibility of a metallic intra-orbital foreign body, do NOT MRI — the magnetic field can move the fragment and blind the patient. Image first with CT (or plain films) to exclude metal.
Metal/glass FBCT yesMRI no
4Proptosis: thyroid eye disease
Thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy) is the commonest cause of bilateral proptosis. CT shows enlarged extraocular muscle bellies that SPARE the tendon insertions — most often the inferior and medial recti ("IM SLow": inferior > medial > superior > lateral). Crowding at the orbital apex can compress the optic nerve.
Tendon sparing distinguishes TED from orbital myositis, which involves the tendon insertion.
🚩
Sight-threatening emergencies. Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis or a subperiosteal abscess, any reduced acuity/colour vision, an RAPD, or a tense proptosis suggesting orbital compartment syndrome / retrobulbar haemorrhage need urgent imaging, IV antibiotics and immediate ophthalmology. Retrobulbar haemorrhage may need emergency lateral canthotomy. A paediatric white-eyed trapdoor blowout with the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia/vomiting) needs urgent surgical release.

High-resolution CT of the temporal (petrous) bones gives fine bony detail of the external, middle and inner ear, the ossicles, mastoid air cells, facial nerve canal and otic capsule. It is the workhorse for cholesteatoma, complicated/chronic otitis media and mastoiditis, conductive hearing loss, temporal bone trauma, pre-cochlear-implant assessment and CSF leak. Read it with a 4-lens approach: soft tissue, bony erosion, air-cell opacification and the fracture plane.
1Cholesteatoma — non-dependent soft tissue with bony erosion
Cholesteatoma is abnormal keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear, usually arising from the pars flaccida (attic) and locally destructive. On CT look for a non-dependent soft-tissue mass in the middle ear/attic filling Prussak's space, with bony erosion as the key feature.
Scutum blunting/erosionOssicular erosionLateral SCC fistulaTegmen/facial canal erosion
Foul otorrhoea + attic crust + soft tissue eroding scutum→Cholesteatoma until proven otherwise
2Mastoiditis — opacified cells & loss of septa
A complication of acute otitis media. CT shows opacified mastoid air cells; the crucial sign is loss of the fine bony septa (coalescent mastoiditis), which may be followed by a subperiosteal abscess.
  • Simple fluid/opacification alone = otomastoiditis, not surgical by itself.
  • Septal breakdown or abscess = coalescent disease needing intervention.
  • Screen for facial palsy, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and intracranial abscess/meningitis.
3Temporal bone fracture — longitudinal vs transverse
Classify the fracture plane relative to the long axis of the petrous bone; each carries a different injury pattern.
↔️Longitudinal (commoner)
Along the long axis. Ossicular disruption → conductive hearing loss; CSF otorrhoea; facial palsy less common and usually delayed.
↕️Transverse
Across the axis, through the otic capsule. Sensorineural loss, vertigo and higher risk of facial nerve injury (often immediate/complete).
Also hunt for ossicular chain disruption and pneumolabyrinth (air in the labyrinth) — a sign of otic capsule breach.
4Structured review checklist
Run the same list every time so nothing is missed.
  • Soft tissue — dependent (effusion) vs non-dependent (cholesteatoma)?
  • Bone — scutum, ossicles, tegmen, facial canal, lateral SCC intact?
  • Air cells — opacified? septa preserved or coalescent?
  • Fracture — plane, ossicles, otic capsule involvement?
🚩
Complications of cholesteatoma or mastoiditis — facial nerve palsy, labyrinthine fistula/vertigo, or intracranial spread (meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, cerebral abscess) — are an emergency needing urgent ENT referral, imaging and surgery. A temporal bone fracture with facial palsy or CSF leak also needs urgent specialist input.

For mastoiditis, opacification alone is not enough; look for loss of bony septa (coalescent). For trauma, remember longitudinal → conductive loss + CSF otorrhoea, transverse → sensorineural loss, vertigo and facial palsy.
Thin-slice CT of the facial bones (with multiplanar reformats and often 3D reconstruction) is the investigation of choice for maxillofacial trauma. It maps the fracture pattern in three dimensions to plan surgical fixation, and detects associated orbital, skull base and C-spine injury that plain films miss.
1Recognise the Le Fort patterns
Le Fort fractures separate the midface from the skull base; by definition all three cross the pterygoid plates, so scroll the axials until you find that constant clue.
🦷Le Fort I
Horizontal across the maxilla above the teeth — a “floating palate”.
🔺Le Fort II
Pyramidal through the nasofrontal region, maxilla and infraorbital rims — a “floating maxilla”.
💀Le Fort III
Craniofacial disjunction across the nasofrontal suture, orbits and zygomatic arches — a “floating face”.
Patterns are often mixed and asymmetric (e.g. Le Fort II on one side, III on the other).
2Spot the ZMC (“tripod”) fracture
The zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture disrupts the cheekbone at its three (really four) attachments: the zygomaticofrontal suture, the zygomatic arch, and the infraorbital rim / anterior maxillary wall.
Cheek flatteningInfraorbital nerve numbnessTrismus
Numb cheek + upper lip after a blow to the malar eminence→Suspect ZMC with infraorbital nerve injury
3Orbital floor, mandible and nasal bones
  • Orbital floor “blowout”: herniation of fat/inferior rectus into the maxillary sinus (“teardrop” sign) — test for diplopia and muscle entrapment.
  • Mandible is a ring bone — fractures are often in two places; if you see one, hunt for a second fracture or a condylar injury.
  • Nasal bones: the commonest facial fracture, best seen on the axial and coronal reformats.
4Clinically correlate the scan
Never read the CT in isolation — document the infraorbital nerve (cheek/upper-lip sensation), the eye (diplopia, entrapment, visual acuity), dental occlusion (malocclusion suggests a displaced maxillary or mandibular fracture), and always the airway and C-spine.
🚩
Facial trauma is an airway threat: brisk bleeding, displaced midface fractures, or a bilateral parasymphyseal “flail” mandible letting the tongue fall back can obstruct rapidly — manage ABC and C-spine first. Heavy midface haemorrhage and CSF rhinorrhoea (base-of-skull injury) need urgent specialist care, and retrobulbar haemorrhage or muscle entrapment threatens vision — a sight-saving emergency.

But score the safety mark first: airway, C-spine and vision take priority over describing the fracture.
A contrast-enhanced CT neck (soft tissue) is the workhorse study for the deep neck. It maps the deep neck spaces, airway, salivary glands, thyroid, lymph nodes and great vessels. Its four big jobs: hunt for a deep neck space abscess, stage head & neck cancer, characterise a neck lump / lymphadenopathy, and assess salivary and thyroid pathology.
1Spot the abscess
A drainable abscess shows a rim-enhancing fluid collection with surrounding fat stranding. This distinguishes a mature collection from early cellulitis / phlegmon (ill-defined, no drainable cavity). Look for gas locules (necrotising infection) and airway narrowing.
Rim enhancementCentral low densityFat strandingGas = necrotising
2Name the deep neck infection
Localise the collection to its space — this drives management and predicts danger.
🦠Peritonsillar (quinsy)
Medial to tonsil; trismus, "hot potato" voice, uvular deviation.
🦠Parapharyngeal
Displaces airway medially; risk to carotid sheath vessels.
🦠Retropharyngeal
"Danger space" — can track down to the mediastinum.
🦠Ludwig's angina
Bilateral submandibular/sublingual cellulitis; odontogenic; tongue elevation, rapid airway loss.
Also scan the internal jugular vein: filling defect + tonsillitis = Lemierre's syndrome (Fusobacterium septic thrombophlebitis).
3Read the nodes for cancer
For a suspicious neck lump, CT defines the primary tumour extent, invasion of cartilage / vessels, and the nodal status for TNM staging.
Round node, central necrosis, lost fatty hilum, extranodal spread→Malignant node
  • Persistent adult neck lump / node (esp. smoker or drinker) → urgent 2-week-wait ENT referral.
  • Triple assessment: examination + imaging + tissue (FNA/core, often US-guided).
4Trace the danger routes
Before signing off, follow the collection caudally and check the vessels — the exam wants the complications, not just the diagnosis.
Mediastinal extensionIJV thrombosis (Lemierre's)Carotid encasementAirway compression
🚩
Airway compromise is an emergency. Stridor, drooling, tripod positioning, or tongue elevation in Ludwig's angina with rapid swelling means the airway comes first — call senior anaesthetics and ENT, give IV antibiotics, and arrange drainage. A retropharyngeal abscess can descend into the mediastinum (mediastinitis), and Lemierre's needs prolonged antibiotics with anticoagulation considered.

A round node with central necrosis and loss of the fatty hilum is malignant until proven otherwise; a persistent adult neck lump = 2-week-wait ENT.
A CT carotid angiogram (CTA) images the carotid and vertebral arteries from the aortic arch to the intracranial circulation using timed IV contrast. Its two finals-critical roles are quantifying carotid stenosis after a TIA or ischaemic stroke to select patients for carotid endarterectomy, and detecting arterial dissection as a cause of stroke in the young.
1When and why it is requested
After a TIA or non-disabling ischaemic stroke in the anterior (carotid territory) circulation, the carotids must be imaged urgently. Doppler ultrasound is first-line; CTA or MRA confirms and quantifies stenosis before surgery. It is also the key test for suspected carotid or vertebral dissection in a young patient with focal neurology.
TIA / anterior strokeSuspected dissectionPre-endarterectomy workup
2Carotid stenosis and stroke prevention
CTA quantifies stenosis by the NASCET method. A symptomatic significant stenosis (commonly ~50–99% per NICE) on the side appropriate to the symptoms should be referred for carotid endarterectomy (CEA), ideally within 2 weeks of symptom onset, alongside best medical therapy. A 100% (fully occluded) carotid is not revascularised, and asymptomatic stenosis is usually managed medically.
🩺Symptomatic 50–99%
Refer for endarterectomy within 2 weeks + best medical therapy.
💊Asymptomatic
Usually medical management; surgery rarely indicated.
⛔100% occluded
Not revascularised — medical therapy only.
Best medical therapy = antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP control, smoking cessation.
3Carotid / vertebral dissection
An intimal tear allows an intramural haematoma to form — a key cause of stroke in the young. It may follow neck trauma or manipulation or be spontaneous (connective tissue disease). On CTA look for a tapered “flame” / string sign of luminal narrowing, an intimal flap, or a false lumen.
Neck pain + partial Horner's + cerebral/retinal ischaemia→Carotid dissection
  • Classic triad: neck/head pain + painful partial Horner's (ptosis + miosis) + ischaemia.
  • Treat with antiplatelet or anticoagulation.
4Reading the images
Trace each vessel from the arch upward. Assess the carotid bifurcation for calcified/soft plaque and measure the residual lumen (NASCET). In dissection, compare the two sides for asymmetric narrowing, a crescentic mural haematoma, or an intimal flap.
Bifurcation plaqueString signIntimal flap
🚩
A TIA or minor stroke with a symptomatic significant carotid stenosis is a stroke-prevention emergency: urgent carotid imaging and referral for endarterectomy within 2 weeks, plus immediate antiplatelet and statin. Separately, a young patient with neck pain and Horner's and focal neurology suggests dissection — needing urgent imaging and antiplatelet/anticoagulation.

Two answers to keep straight: an older patient post-TIA with a symptomatic 50–99% stenosis on the symptomatic side → carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks + best medical therapy (never revascularise a 100% occlusion or an asymptomatic stenosis). A young patient with neck pain + painful partial Horner's → dissection, look for the string sign / intimal flap on CTA and treat with antiplatelet or anticoagulation.
CT__Spine:
The CT cervical spine is the first-line imaging for suspected significant C-spine injury in trauma — it is far more sensitive than plain radiographs and detects fractures plain films miss. The clinical question splits in two: who needs imaging (decision rules) and what to look for (named fractures, alignment, prevertebral tissues). MRI is added when the cord, ligaments or discs need assessing.
1Who needs the CT — decision rules
Two validated rules select patients: the Canadian C-spine rule and NEXUS criteria allow low-risk patients to be cleared clinically without imaging. Image if any high-risk factor is present, per NICE/Canadian rule:
Age ≥65Dangerous mechanismParaesthesiae in limbsCannot rotate neck 45° each way
High-risk factor, reduced GCS or older patient→CT preferred over plain films
2Named upper C-spine fractures
These are the exam favourites — learn the mechanism for each:
🦴Jefferson (C1)
C1 burst fracture from axial load; lateral mass spread on the peg view/CT.
🦷Odontoid peg (C2)
Dens fracture; Anderson–D'Alonzo type II at the base is commonest and unstable.
⚖️Hangman's (C2)
Traumatic spondylolisthesis — bilateral pars/pedicle fracture from hyperextension.
Also consider facet dislocations, teardrop fractures and clay-shoveler's (C7 spinous process).
3Systematic review — alignment & soft tissues
Do not just look for the fracture; check every vertebra and the lines:
  • Anterior and posterior vertebral lines — should be smooth, unbroken curves.
  • Spinolaminar line — step-off suggests dislocation.
  • Prevertebral soft tissue swelling — a subtle clue to occult fracture/haematoma.
  • Assess each vertebral body height and the atlanto-dental interval.
4Stability, cord and the role of MRI
A fracture may be stable or unstable. CT shows bone superbly but not the cord — add MRI to assess the spinal cord, ligaments and discs. Classic trap: central cord syndrome in an elderly patient after a hyperextension injury with no fracture on CT. Immobilise the whole spine until formally cleared.
Neurology or ligamentous injury suspected, normal CT→MRI for cord & ligaments
🚩
Any suspected unstable C-spine injury or cord compromise (limb neurology, priapism, neurogenic shock) needs strict immobilisation (hard collar, blocks, log-roll), urgent CT ± MRI and spinal team referral. Never clear the C-spine clinically in an obtunded, intoxicated or distracting-injury patient — image them. Beware ankylosing spondylitis / DISH, where trivial trauma causes unstable transverse fractures.

🎓 Exam pearl. If asked "which investigation first?" in blunt trauma with any high-risk factor, reduced GCS or age ≥65, the answer is CT cervical spine — not plain films. Use the Canadian C-spine rule / NEXUS to decide who can be cleared without imaging, reserve MRI for cord and ligamentous injury (including the fracture-negative central cord syndrome), and never clinically clear the neck of an obtunded patient.
CT is the first-line imaging for suspected thoracic spine trauma, and thoracic fractures are frequently first characterised on a trauma CT chest/abdomen. The thoracic and lumbar spine are usually reviewed together on reformatted (reconstructed) images. Always assess alignment, the three columns, canal compromise, and the thoracolumbar junction (T11–L2) — the biomechanical transition zone and the commonest site of injury.
1The 3-column concept & stability
Denis divides the spine into anterior, middle and posterior columns. Involvement of ≥2 columns — especially the middle column — implies instability. The middle column (posterior vertebral body wall + posterior longitudinal ligament) is the key structure: an intact middle column usually means a stable injury.
Middle column involved→Assume unstable until proven otherwise
2Recognise the key fracture patterns
Match the pattern to the mechanism and stability:
🔻Wedge compression
Anterior column only, loss of anterior vertebral height. Usually stable.
💥Burst
Axial load, anterior + middle columns, retropulsion into canal → cord risk. Unstable.
🪢Chance (seat-belt)
Horizontal flexion-distraction through all 3 columns. Look for intra-abdominal injury.
🔀Fracture-dislocation
Failure of all columns with translation/rotation. The most unstable pattern.
3Systematic review checklist
Work through each level looking for:
  • Alignment — step, translation or focal kyphosis.
  • Retropulsion — bone fragment displaced posteriorly into the spinal canal.
  • Height loss — anterior wedging vs whole-body collapse.
  • Posterior element fractures (pedicles, laminae, spinous processes).
AlignmentRetropulsionCanalKyphosis
4Atraumatic & pathological collapse
Not all collapse is trauma. Osteoporotic collapse is common in the elderly, but suspect a pathological (malignant) cause — metastasis or myeloma — if there is bony destruction, a soft-tissue mass, posterior wall involvement or an atypical level. MRI whole spine is the key next step to assess marrow and exclude cord compression.
CT shows bony detail; MRI shows the cord, marrow and ligaments.
🚩
A burst fracture with retropulsion/canal compromise, or any fracture with neurology, risks spinal cord injury — immobilise, add MRI to assess the cord and refer to spinal surgery. A Chance (seat-belt) fracture mandates a search for intra-abdominal injury (bowel, mesenteric, pancreatic). New atraumatic/pathological collapse with back pain and red flags needs urgent work-up for malignancy and cord compression.

🎓 Exam pearl. The middle column is the examiner's favourite: intact = stable, involved = unstable. A burst differs from a simple wedge by middle-column failure with retropulsion. A Chance fracture = seat-belt lap injury → always image the abdomen. Reach for MRI whenever you suspect cord injury or pathological/malignant collapse.
A CT lumbar spine is the workhorse for bony pathology of the lower back — trauma, the bony canal and facet joints, spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis and pre-operative planning. But remember the golden rule: for the disc, nerve roots and especially cauda equina syndrome, MRI is the investigation of choice — CT poorly shows the neural elements and soft-tissue disc. CT is reserved for bony assessment or when MRI is contraindicated.
1Bone first — trauma & fractures
CT excels at cortical and trabecular detail. In trauma look for the burst fracture (axial load with retropulsion of a bony fragment into the canal — assess canal compromise) and the anterior wedge compression fracture. Distinguish benign osteoporotic collapse from pathological (malignant) collapse — the latter shows posterior cortex/pedicle destruction and a soft-tissue mass.
BurstWedgeRetropulsionCanal %
2Pars defect & the slip
Spondylolysis is a defect (stress fracture) of the pars interarticularis — the classic "Scottie dog collar" sign on oblique/CT reconstructions. Bilateral pars defects allow a vertebra to slide forwards on the one below — spondylolisthesis (classically L5 on S1). CT grades the slip and the bony anatomy for surgical planning.
Bilateral pars defect→forward vertebral slip (spondylolisthesis)
3Degenerative change & stenosis
Age brings facet arthropathy, osteophytes and ligamentum flavum thickening that narrow the canal — spinal (canal) stenosis. Clinically this causes neurogenic claudication: bilateral leg pain/heaviness on walking, eased by flexion/sitting (leaning on a trolley) — unlike vascular claudication which eases simply by stopping.
🦴Facet arthropathy
Hypertrophied facet joints narrow the lateral recess and canal.
🚶Neurogenic claudication
Leg pain walking, relieved by flexion/sitting.
4Know CT's blind spot — the neural elements
CT is relatively poor at showing the soft-tissue disc, nerve roots and conus/cauda equina. If the clinical question is disc prolapse, radiculopathy or — critically — cauda equina syndrome, request an urgent MRI, not a CT. Reserve CT for bone or where MRI is contraindicated (e.g. certain pacemakers, metalwork).
CT myelography is an alternative when MRI cannot be done and neural detail is essential.
🚩
Back pain with any cauda equina red flags — saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, bilateral sciatica, reduced anal tone — is a surgical emergency: request urgent MRI whole spine (NOT CT) and make an immediate spinal referral for decompression. Also flag sinister features of malignancy or infection: weight loss, fever, night pain, thoracic pain, immunosuppression or IVDU (think discitis/epidural abscess).

Match modality to the question: CT = bone (fractures, pars defect, spondylolisthesis, bony canal, pre-op planning), MRI = soft tissue/neural (disc, nerve roots, cord/conus, cauda equina, infection, tumour). Suspected cauda equina syndrome is always an urgent MRI plus emergency spinal referral — never delay for or settle for a CT.
CT whole spine images the entire vertebral column (occiput to coccyx) in one study, usually reconstructed from a trauma "pan-scan" (CT head/C-spine + chest/abdomen/pelvis). Its core rationale: non-contiguous (multiple-level) spinal fractures occur in ~10–15% of patients who have one spinal fracture, so finding a single fracture mandates imaging the whole spine to catch a second, more distant injury.
1Who gets a whole-spine CT?
Reserve for significant / high-energy trauma and situations where the spine cannot be cleared clinically.
🦴Known fracture
One vertebral fracture found → image the whole spine to find a second (~10–15%).
🚗High energy
RTC, fall from height, multi-region injury or a distracting injury.
😵Unclearable
Reduced GCS, obtunded or intoxicated — cannot be examined reliably.
⚡Neurology / rigid spine
Any neuro signs; or ankylosing spondylitis / DISH even after trivial trauma.
2Systematic interpretation
Whole-spine reformats are read across every level, not just the injured region.
AlignmentBonesCord/canalDiscs/soft tissue
  • Trace the anterior and posterior vertebral lines for step-offs and malalignment.
  • Assess vertebral body height loss, retropulsion into the canal and facet integrity.
  • Prevertebral soft-tissue swelling is a clue to occult injury.
One fracture seen→actively hunt for a second, non-contiguous level
3When to add MRI
CT is excellent for bone but MRI is added for soft tissue and cord.
  • Any neurological deficit or suspected cord / ligamentous injury.
  • SCIWORA — spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality (esp. children).
  • To help clear the obtunded patient's C-spine per local protocol.
4Management principles
ATLS approach with C-spine control during airway management; maintain full spinal precautions (collar, blocks, log-roll, nurse flat) until cleared.
Hypotension + bradycardia in high cord injury→think neurogenic shock, not just haemorrhage
Refer early to spinal / neurosurgery; exclude coexisting haemorrhagic shock.
🚩
A spinal fracture at one level mandates whole-spine imaging — ~10–15% harbour a second, non-contiguous fracture. An obtunded, intoxicated or neurologically abnormal patient cannot be cleared clinically and must be immobilised and imaged. In ankylosing spondylitis / DISH even trivial trauma can cause a highly unstable transverse fracture that is easily missed — have a very low threshold to scan the whole spine.

Remember the unclearable patient (low GCS, intoxicated), the rigid ankylosing / DISH spine that fractures with trivial force, and neurogenic shock (hypotension WITH bradycardia) as the pattern that distinguishes cord injury from bleeding.
CT__Chest / Lung:
Contrast-enhanced CT chest (with IV iodinated contrast) is the general workhorse for the mediastinum, hila, pleura, chest wall and vessels. It characterises a mediastinal or hilar mass, lymphadenopathy, a lung mass, pleural disease (effusion, empyema, malignant thickening, mesothelioma), infection/abscess, and vascular structures. Dedicated protocols — CTPA for PE, HRCT for interstitial lung disease — are separate studies.
1Review on all three windows
Never read a CT chest on one window. Systematically toggle through each.
Lung windowMediastinal/soft-tissueBone window
  • Lung windows — parenchyma: nodules, consolidation, emphysema, bronchiectasis.
  • Mediastinal windows — nodes, masses, vessels and pleura (where IV contrast pays off).
  • Bone windows — lytic/sclerotic mets, fractures, rib destruction.
2Localise a mediastinal mass by compartment
Compartment predicts the differential. The classic anterior mediastinal "4 Ts":
🫀Thymoma
Assoc. myasthenia gravis; anterior mass.
🧬Teratoma
Germ-cell tumour; fat/calcium.
🦋Thyroid
Retrosternal goitre; continuous with neck.
🩸"Terrible" lymphoma
Bulky nodal mass in young/older adult.
Middle — lymphadenopathy, bronchogenic/pericardial cysts, vascular. Posterior — neurogenic tumours (nerve sheath, ganglion).
3Assess lymphadenopathy — benign vs malignant
Contrast helps distinguish nodes from vessels and shows necrosis.
Node >1 cm short axis, necrotic centre, matted→Suspicious — malignancy/TB
Symmetrical bilateral hilar (sarcoid "1-2-3")→Often benign/sarcoidosis
  • Distribution helps stage cancer and pattern sarcoid, TB and lymphoma.
4Characterise the pleura + check contrast safety
Contrast is key for pleural enhancement.
Nodular/circumferential thickeningMediastinal pleura involvedThickening >1 cm
  • These four suggest malignant pleural disease — mesothelioma (asbestos exposure).
  • Empyema — the "split pleura" sign: enhancing, thickened visceral and parietal pleura around a loculated collection.
  • Before contrast: check renal function (eGFR), contrast allergy and metformin.
🚩
A mediastinal mass causing superior vena cava obstruction (facial/arm swelling, distended chest-wall veins, plethora — often lung cancer or lymphoma) is an oncological emergency needing urgent imaging and treatment. A large mass compressing the trachea/airway threatens breathing. Any suspected malignancy needs an urgent MDT referral and tissue diagnosis.

Anchor four lenses: the anterior mediastinal "4 Ts" (Thymoma, Teratoma, Thyroid, "Terrible" lymphoma); malignant vs benign lymphadenopathy (>1 cm short axis, necrosis, distribution); pleural features (mesothelioma's circumferential thickening, empyema's split-pleura sign); and contrast safety (eGFR, allergy, metformin). Spot SVC obstruction and airway compression as emergencies.
A non-contrast CT chest is chosen when IV contrast is unnecessary or contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy). Its core roles are characterising and following up a pulmonary nodule, assessing parenchymal disease (emphysema, bronchiectasis, some infection) and quantifying coronary calcium. Because CT delivers a significant radiation dose, every scan must be justified and run on the lowest appropriate protocol (ALARA).
1Know when to drop the contrast
Reach for non-contrast CT when contrast adds little or is contraindicated. Typical triggers: eGFR impairment, previous contrast allergy, and imaging aimed purely at lung parenchyma or nodules rather than vessels/mediastinal enhancement.
Renal impairmentContrast allergyNodule follow-upEmphysema / bronchiectasis
2Assess the solitary pulmonary nodule
The finals-favourite task. Work through five features:
  • Size — larger nodules carry higher malignant risk.
  • Margins — spiculated/irregular = suspicious; smooth = often benign.
  • Calcification — central, laminated, popcorn (hamartoma) or diffuse = benign; eccentric or absent = worrying.
  • Fat — intralesional fat suggests a benign hamartoma.
  • Growth — compare with prior scans; stable ≥2 years is reassuring.
Small, smooth, benign calcification, stable ≥2 yrs→Benign — reassure
3Risk-stratify and plan follow-up
UK BTS nodule guidelines combine size and risk models (Brock, Herder) to decide the next step: CT surveillance, PET-CT or biopsy. Low-dose non-contrast CT is the standard for nodule surveillance and screening, keeping cumulative dose down.
🫁CT surveillance
Small/low-risk nodules — interval low-dose CT to check growth.
🔬PET-CT
Higher-risk / larger nodules — assess metabolic activity.
🩸Biopsy / MDT
Suspicious lesion — tissue diagnosis via respiratory MDT.
4Recognise the benign incidentals
Common non-contrast findings you should name and not over-investigate:
  • Emphysema — low-attenuation destruction ± bullae.
  • Calcified granulomata — old TB or histoplasmosis.
  • Pleural plaques — calcified, benign; a marker of asbestos exposure.
Pleural plaques signal exposure, not disease — but prompt a review for mesothelioma symptoms.
🚩
A nodule with malignant features — spiculation, large or growing, upper lobe, in an older patient or smoker — needs prompt work-up: PET-CT/biopsy, respiratory MDT and a 2-week-wait referral if lung cancer is suspected. Never dismiss a growing or spiculated nodule.

Benign calcification (central/laminated/popcorn/diffuse), intralesional fat, or stability ≥2 years point to benign; spiculation, growth or upper-lobe location in a smoker demand PET-CT/biopsy and MDT. Choose non-contrast CT when contrast is contraindicated or unneeded, and always justify the dose under ALARA.
High-Resolution CT (HRCT) uses thin (1–1.5 mm) slices with a high-spatial-frequency reconstruction algorithm to display fine lung architecture. It is the investigation of choice for diffuse parenchymal (interstitial) lung disease and bronchiectasis, and is usually performed non-contrast. Always read it alongside lung function (restrictive spirometry, reduced TLCO) and the ILD MDT.
1The UIP pattern = IPF
The usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern is the finals-favourite. Look for peripheral/subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis. This pattern, in the right clinical context, supports idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).
SubpleuralBasalHoneycombingTraction bronchiectasis
2Ground-glass = active / inflammatory
Ground-glass opacification is a hazy increased attenuation that does not obscure the underlying vessels (unlike consolidation). It suggests active alveolitis / inflammation and is potentially treatable/reversible.
Ground-glass + hypoxia in immunocompromised→think PCP / drug pneumonitis
  • Infection (PCP, viral)
  • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis and NSIP
  • Early/active fibrosing lung disease
3Bronchiectasis & the signet-ring sign
Bronchiectasis is irreversible bronchial dilatation. The hallmark is the signet-ring sign — the dilated bronchus is wider than its accompanying artery. Also look for tram-track lines, wall thickening and lack of tapering towards the periphery.
🫁Causes
CF, post-infective, ABPA, immunodeficiency
4Zone of fibrosis + other patterns
The zone of fibrosis narrows the differential. Mosaic attenuation points to small-airways disease; nodules can be perilymphatic (sarcoid) or random/miliary (TB).
UPPER: TB, sarcoid, HP, ank spond, radiation, silicosis/coal
LOWER: IPF, asbestosis, connective tissue disease, drugs (methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin)
Always ask about drugs and occupation — both change the whole differential.
🚩
A UIP/IPF pattern carries a poor prognosis and needs ILD MDT referral for antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib). An acute exacerbation of ILD, or new widespread ground-glass with hypoxia (e.g. PCP in the immunocompromised, or drug-induced pneumonitis), needs urgent treatment — always consider a drug cause and stop the culprit.

Fix the zone: upper-zone fibrosis screams TB/sarcoid/HP, lower-zone screams IPF/asbestosis/CTD/drugs. HRCT is non-contrast — correlate with restrictive lung function, a reduced TLCO and the MDT.
A CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA) times an IV contrast bolus to opacify the pulmonary arteries and is the first-line definitive test for pulmonary embolism (PE). A PE appears as a filling defect within a contrast-opacified pulmonary artery; a large clot straddling the bifurcation is a saddle embolus. Reading a CTPA well means answering four questions: is there a clot, does the pathway justify the scan, is the right heart strained, and how do we treat.
1Confirm the diagnosis — the filling defect
On a CTPA a PE is a filling defect: a dark, non-opacified thrombus outlined by bright contrast within a pulmonary artery. A clot straddling the main bifurcation is a saddle embolus. CTPA is first-line and definitive for PE — it both confirms the clot and shows its distribution (central vs segmental/subsegmental).
Filling defectSaddle embolusWedge infarct
2Justify the scan — the Wells pathway
NICE uses the two-level Wells score to decide who gets a CTPA:
PE LIKELY (Wells >4)→immediate CTPA (interim anticoagulation if delay)
PE UNLIKELY (Wells ≤4)→D-dimer: if raised → CTPA; if normal → PE excluded
D-dimer is sensitive but not specific — also raised in infection, malignancy, pregnancy and post-op. If CTPA is contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy) or in pregnancy, a V/Q (ventilation-perfusion) scan is the alternative.
3Grade the severity — right heart strain
A large, haemodynamically significant PE strains the right ventricle. Look for RV dilatation, an RV:LV ratio >1, and septal bowing toward the left ventricle; a peripheral wedge infarct may also be seen. Correlate with the ECG (sinus tachycardia is commonest; S1Q3T3 is classic but rare) and bedside echo in massive PE.
🫀RV dilatation
RV:LV ratio >1 marks a large, high-risk PE.
↔️Septal bowing
Interventricular septum pushed toward the LV.
4Treat — anticoagulation and beyond
Confirmed PE is treated with anticoagulation — a DOAC first-line per NICE (e.g. apixaban, rivaroxaban). A massive PE with haemodynamic instability (hypotension/shock) is an emergency requiring thrombolysis (e.g. alteplase) or surgical/catheter embolectomy.
  • Stable PE → DOAC first-line.
  • Massive/unstable PE → thrombolysis or embolectomy.
🚩
A massive PE with haemodynamic instability (hypotension, syncope, cardiac arrest — often PEA) is a peri-arrest emergency needing resuscitation and thrombolysis. Signs of right heart strain on CTPA or echo mark a high-risk PE. Consider PE in any breathless, hypoxic or collapsed patient with risk factors.

🎓 Exam pearl. If a stem gives Wells >4 (PE likely), go straight to CTPA — do NOT order a D-dimer first. D-dimer only belongs in the PE unlikely (Wells ≤4) arm. Reach for a V/Q scan when CTPA is contraindicated by renal impairment, contrast allergy or pregnancy. On the scan, a filling defect confirms PE and RV:LV >1 flags a high-risk PE that may need thrombolysis.
A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and upper abdomen (to include the liver and adrenals) is the first-line staging investigation for confirmed or suspected lung cancer. It delivers TNM staging — tumour size and local invasion (T), nodal spread (N) and distant metastases (M) — and drives every downstream decision about resectability and treatment.
1Read the CT for TNM
Assess T — tumour size and local invasion of chest wall, mediastinum, diaphragm and any satellite nodules. Assess N — hilar and mediastinal nodes, pathological if >1 cm short axis. Assess M — scan through the liver and adrenals (a common metastatic site), plus bone and the contralateral lung; the brain needs dedicated contrast CT or MRI head, not the chest CT.
Node >1 cm short axis→Suspicious — needs tissue confirmation
2Follow the staging pathway
The sequence is CT chest/abdomen → PET-CT → tissue diagnosis → MDT. PET-CT is a functional scan that upstages disease by detecting occult nodal or distant metastases and characterises the primary and nodes — but it does not image the brain.
CTPET-CTEBUS / biopsyMDT
3Get tissue and confirm N stage
Bronchoscopy / EBUS-TBNA samples central lesions and mediastinal nodes; CT-guided biopsy is used for peripheral lesions. EBUS-TBNA confirms the N stage, which is crucial for resectability — mediastinal nodal involvement or invasion often renders a tumour inoperable.
4Let the stage steer treatment
The treatment split depends on histology and stage:
🫁NSCLC — early / operable
Surgery ± adjuvant therapy.
🎯NSCLC — locally advanced
Chemoradiotherapy ± immunotherapy.
💊NSCLC — metastatic
Systemic / palliative therapy.
⚡SCLC
Usually disseminated at presentation → chemotherapy (limited vs extensive stage).
🚩
Red-flag lung cancer features — haemoptysis, weight loss, a persistent cough or CXR abnormality in a smoker, finger clubbing or a cervical/supraclavicular node — need an urgent 2-week-wait referral and staging CT. A Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumour causing Horner's syndrome, arm pain or T1 wasting, or SVC obstruction, needs urgent attention. Always hunt for metastatic sites: adrenal, liver, bone and brain.

🎓 Exam pearl. Staging CT chest/abdomen gives the TNM and must cover liver and adrenals (common mets, alongside bone and brain). Learn the pathway: CT → PET-CT → EBUS/biopsy → MDT. Mediastinal nodal involvement is the classic driver of inoperability, and remember the histology split — resectable NSCLC gets surgery, while SCLC is usually disseminated and treated with chemotherapy. PET-CT and EBUS-TBNA do not assess the brain, which needs dedicated CT/MRI head.
A low-dose CT (LDCT) chest is a reduced-radiation, non-contrast CT used for lung cancer screening in high-risk individuals. The aim is to detect cancer at an earlier, more curable (operable) stage and so reduce lung-cancer mortality. It is offered to asymptomatic high-risk people — not as a work-up for symptoms.
1Why it exists — the evidence
Two large randomised trials underpin LDCT screening: the US NLST and the European NELSON. Both showed that screening high-risk smokers with LDCT reduces lung-cancer mortality (~20% relative reduction in NLST) versus no screening or chest X-ray. Lung cancer is common, has a poor overall prognosis when symptomatic, but is far more curable when found early and small — the rationale for catching it before symptoms appear.
NLST (US)NELSON (Europe)~20% mortality ↓
2The UK programme — Targeted Lung Health Checks
The NHS Targeted Lung Health Check (TLHC) / lung cancer screening programme invites people aged roughly 55–74 who are current or ex-smokers (ever-smokers). A risk assessment using validated models (e.g. PLCOm2012) identifies those at high enough risk to benefit; eligible people are offered LDCT, typically repeated at intervals if the initial scan is negative. Crucially it is bundled with smoking cessation support.
Ever-smoker, age 55–74, high-risk on model→Invite for LDCT + cessation
3Screening principles & harms
LDCT screening satisfies the Wilson–Jungner criteria: an important condition with a recognisable early/latent stage, an acceptable test, effective treatment for early disease, and benefits that outweigh harms. But screening is never harm-free:
  • False positives — benign nodules cause anxiety and drive further tests/biopsy risk
  • Overdiagnosis — detection of indolent cancers that would never have caused harm
  • Radiation exposure (low but not zero) and incidental findings elsewhere
🫁Benefit
Earlier-stage, operable cancer → lower lung-cancer mortality
⚠️Harm
False positives, overdiagnosis, radiation, incidentalomas
4What happens to a detected nodule
Screen-detected nodules are managed by standardised protocols driven by size and growth. Small, low-risk nodules go to interval surveillance LDCT to assess for growth; larger or growing/higher-risk nodules are worked up with PET-CT and/or biopsy and referred to the lung MDT. This structured approach limits unnecessary invasive procedures while catching genuine cancers.
Size/growth → surveillancePET-CTBiopsy / MDT
🚩
Screening is only for the asymptomatic high-risk population. A person with symptoms of possible lung cancer — haemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, persistent/changing cough, or a new chest X-ray change — must go on the urgent (2-week-wait) symptomatic cancer pathway, NOT routine screening. Likewise, a screen-detected suspicious nodule needs prompt MDT work-up, not deferral.

🎓 Exam pearl. Four-lens capstone: LDCT screening of high-risk ever-smokers aged ~55–74 reduces lung-cancer mortality (evidence: NLST/NELSON; delivered in the UK via Targeted Lung Health Checks with cessation support). It meets Wilson–Jungner criteria but carries real harms — false positives, overdiagnosis, radiation, incidentalomas. Nodules follow standardised size/growth management (surveillance LDCT → PET-CT/biopsy). The classic finals distinction: screening = asymptomatic; a symptomatic patient belongs on the 2-week-wait pathway.

CT coronary angiography (CTCA) is a contrast-enhanced, ECG-gated CT of the coronary arteries. Per updated NICE (CG95) guidance it is the first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected coronary/anginal origin — offered to anyone with typical or atypical angina, or non-anginal chest pain plus an abnormal resting ECG (e.g. pathological Q waves). It excels at ruling out disease thanks to its very high negative predictive value.
1When to offer it (NICE first-line)
Offer CTCA as the first-line test for stable chest pain when any of the following apply:
  • Typical angina (all 3 features: constricting discomfort, provoked by exertion, relieved by rest/GTN).
  • Atypical angina (2 of 3 features).
  • Non-anginal chest pain (0–1 features) but an abnormal resting ECG (e.g. Q waves, ST/T changes, LBBB).
Stable exertional chest pain→CTCA first-line, not exercise ECG
2What it shows & why it is powerful
CTCA images both the lumen and the vessel wall, so it detects calcified and non-calcified (soft) plaque and can be paired with a coronary calcium score.
✅High negative predictive value
A normal CTCA effectively excludes significant obstructive coronary artery disease — its greatest strength is ruling out CAD.
🔬Lumen + plaque
Grades luminal stenosis and characterises plaque; adds a calcium score for risk stratification.
3Interpreting the result
Assess stenosis in each major vessel — LAD, LCx, RCA and left main.
  • Normal / minor disease → CAD excluded, no further cardiac imaging.
  • Possible significant stenosis (~50–70%+) → functional testing (stress perfusion imaging) or invasive coronary angiography ± revascularisation (PCI/CABG).
  • Left main or proximal multi-vessel disease → prognostically important, prompt cardiology referral.
LADLCxRCALeft main
4Practical prerequisites
To get diagnostic images you need a slow, regular heart rate (often beta-blockers given, target ~<60–65 bpm) and a reliable breath-hold. IV iodinated contrast is used, so check renal function and allergy status. GTN may be given to dilate the coronaries.
Fast/irregular rhythm (e.g. AF) or heavy calcification can degrade image quality.
🚩
CTCA is NOT the test for suspected acute coronary syndrome. Acute cardiac-sounding chest pain needs ECG + troponin and the ACS pathway (primary PCI for STEMI) — not CTCA. If CTCA reveals left main or proximal multi-vessel disease, make an urgent cardiology referral.

📷 Image placeholder — 3D volume-rendered CTCA reconstruction of the coronary tree (LAD, LCx, RCA arising from the aortic root) for overall anatomical orientation.
🎓 Exam pearl. CTCA is NICE first-line for stable chest pain (typical/atypical angina, or non-anginal pain with an abnormal ECG). Its killer strength is a high negative predictive value — a normal scan excludes obstructive CAD. It shows lumen and plaque (± calcium score), needs a controlled slow heart rate and IV contrast, and is never the primary test for ACS (that is ECG/troponin/PCI).
The coronary artery calcium (CAC) score is a non-contrast, ECG-gated CT that quantifies calcified atherosclerotic plaque in the coronary arteries using the Agatston score. Calcium is a marker of the overall atherosclerotic burden — it is a low-dose test used to refine cardiovascular risk, not a test for acute chest pain.
1What it measures
A non-contrast, ECG-gated CT detects calcium within the coronary arteries. Each calcified focus is scored by area and peak density, summed to give the Agatston score. Because calcium only forms in atherosclerotic plaque, the score is a direct marker of total plaque burden.
No iodinated contrast is given — this keeps the dose low but means the lumen and soft plaque are not seen.
2Agatston score bands
Learn the four risk bands:
🫀0
No identifiable calcified plaque — very low risk of a coronary event; strong negative predictive value.
🫀1–99
Mild calcification / plaque burden.
🫀100–399
Moderate calcification.
🫀≥400
Extensive calcification — high risk; warrants aggressive risk-factor and statin management.
Score of 0→very low event risk over the next several years
3When it is used
  • Reported alongside / derived from a CTCA in the assessment of stable chest pain.
  • To refine cardiovascular risk in selected asymptomatic / intermediate-risk people.
  • To support a statin decision when the calculated risk is uncertain.
Non-contrastECG-gatedLow-dose
4Key limitation
The score reflects calcified plaque only. Young patients can have soft (non-calcified) plaque causing stenosis with a low or zero calcium score, and a high score does not prove obstructive stenosis — that needs CTCA (contrast: shows lumen, stenosis and soft plaque) or functional testing.
High score, no lumen data→go on to CTCA / functional test to assess flow limitation
🚩
A calcium score is a risk / burden marker, NOT a test for acute chest pain. Acute cardiac chest pain needs the ECG / troponin / ACS pathway, not calcium scoring. A high score in a symptomatic patient warrants further assessment (CTCA / functional testing) and aggressive risk-factor and statin management — but the score alone does not diagnose a flow-limiting stenosis.

🎓 Exam pearl. The Agatston / calcium score is a non-contrast, ECG-gated, low-dose CT quantifying calcified plaque burden (0 = very low risk, ≥400 = high risk). Use it to refine cardiovascular risk and support statin decisions — but remember it images calcified plaque only: soft plaque and stenosis need CTCA / functional testing, and it is never the test for acute chest pain.
The CT aortogram (CT angiography of the aorta, arterial-phase IV contrast) is the definitive test for the acute aortic syndromes and for aortic aneurysm. Its main jobs are to diagnose aortic dissection, aneurysm (thoracic/abdominal ± rupture), traumatic aortic injury, intramural haematoma and penetrating aortic ulcer — reviewed here through a 4-lens lens: what it looks for, the classic presentations, the emergencies, and the one situation where you must NOT wait for it.
1What the CT aortogram is looking for
Arterial-phase contrast opacifies the lumen so you can see the vessel wall and any breach. Key targets:
  • Dissection — an intimal flap and false lumen.
  • Aneurysm — abnormal dilatation, and whether it has ruptured.
  • Intramural haematoma / penetrating ulcer / traumatic injury — the other acute aortic syndromes.
Arterial phaseWhole aorta root→iliacsMultiplanar
2Aortic dissection — flap, false lumen, Stanford
An intimal tear lets blood track into the media, creating a false lumen. CT shows an intimal flap separating true and false lumina. Classify by Stanford:
🩸Type A
Involves the ascending aorta (± arch/descending). Surgical emergency — risk of tamponade, aortic regurgitation, coronary/cerebral malperfusion.
💊Type B
Descending only (distal to left subclavian). Usually medical management — strict BP/HR control (e.g. IV labetalol) unless complicated.
Sudden tearing chest/interscapular pain + inter-arm BP difference + wide mediastinum→Suspect dissection — CT aortogram
Risk factors: hypertension, connective tissue disease (Marfan), bicuspid aortic valve.
3Aneurysm & rupture — AAA
An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is an infrarenal aorta ≥3 cm; rupture risk rises with size, with elective repair usually considered around 5.5 cm (or rapidly growing/symptomatic). A ruptured AAA is catastrophic — sudden abdominal/back pain, a pulsatile mass, and hypotension/collapse.
Stable patient, known/suspected AAA→Urgent CT aortogram to confirm & plan (EVAR vs open)
Unstable patient, known/suspected ruptured AAA→Straight to theatre — do NOT delay for imaging
UK AAA screening: one-off ultrasound for men at age 65.
4Putting it together — the 4 lenses
A single CT aortogram answers: is there a dissection (intimal flap/false lumen; Stanford A = ascending = surgery, B = descending = medical), and is there an aneurysm or rupture. Marry the film to the classic presentations — tearing pain with inter-arm BP difference for dissection, the pain + pulsatile mass + hypotension triad for ruptured AAA — and remember the emergency exception: an unstable ruptured AAA bypasses the scanner.
Dissection?Aneurysm/rupture?Presentation fit?Stable enough to scan?
🚩
Acute Type A dissection and ruptured AAA are surgical emergencies. Resuscitate, control BP in dissection (target with IV labetalol), and get urgent cardiothoracic/vascular surgery. An unstable ruptured AAA goes straight to theatre — never delay for a CT. Never miss a wide mediastinum, tearing pain, or an inter-arm BP difference.
